name: Sara Chen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I play hand drum at a community arts centre, record slow practice beats and help the senior tutor with a beginner class. I worked in a laundry until five years ago and left school after secondary level, so I am still learning the music and I do not call myself a lead teacher.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What makes this work important at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner and I have grown children, but we still pay rent and groceries from our own wages. Retirement is getting closer at 58, and we have less than a month of expenses saved; I do not know what pension income, if any, I can count on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the arts centre that a faster attendance sheet is fine, but children still need a person keeping the beat. I would ask which Friday sessions are paid before promising to be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings would not cover one empty month, and I earn less than most musicians. There are few similar posts nearby, so ordinary cancelled classes already make me nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would keep the paid drum class, the three supervised beginner pupils and the simple practice recordings the centre buys. I would ask the manager for next month’s paid sessions in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even if AI fizzles. At 58, a cancelled month is harder to replace than a broken drum skin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when a class was cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hall closed for a water leak and we lost the class fee. I would ask the centre for a written cancellation payment before the next term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would talk to them, but they have their own bills. I cannot plan a class around money they have not offered.

say: I would welcome **faster attendance sheets** while retaining human class support.
I would ask which **Friday sessions** are paid before promising my time.
think: Our **under-one-month reserve** cannot cover a long class gap.
Few **nearby posts** would replace this lower musician pay.
do: Keep **paid drum classes**, supervised pupils and centre recordings this week.
Request **written paid sessions** and a cancellation fee before next term.
feel: I feel **anxious** about existing cancelled classes and thin savings.
S0.quote: At 58, a cancelled month is harder to replace than a broken drum skin.
fieldNote: She is a **junior musician** after a laundry career, with little savings and uncertain retirement income.
Her **regular classes** depend on written paid sessions, not assumed family help.

steps.text: Keep paid hand-drum class, supervised pupils and centre recordings this week
Request written paid Fridays and cancellation fee before next term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre committee that software can make a practice beat, but the assistant still watches which child is lost. I would ask the workers’ association to protect paid class preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The practice recordings are about a quarter of my small pay. A cheap generated beat could take them, and I cannot easily add another class when the senior tutor sets the timetable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would take the recording invoices to the workers’ association and ask the centre for written paid preparation and class hours. If recording hours fall in the first year, I would keep the supervised pupils and apply for a posted paid community-music assistant job only if my secondary schooling and experience qualify, written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the hours fit my partner’s shared transport; I would stay until an offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about losing the recording fees. I have never used AI, and I would not pretend I can teach a new system in a weekend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you learn the centre’s AI beat maker?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if they offer paid training, approve local storage and let me test my own nameless recording while the senior tutor checks the rhythm by ear. I would stop if the beat changes or the file leaves the centre, but I am not signing up to test it yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there is only a rumour of another job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep this class. I need a real paid vacancy and written hours before I apply.

say: I would ask the **workers’ association** to protect paid preparation.
I would tell the committee **human class support** still matters.
think: Generated **practice beats** could remove a quarter of my pay.
The **senior tutor** controls whether more classes can replace those hours.
do: Bring **recording invoices** to the association and request written paid class preparation.
Apply for a **posted assistant job** if recording hours fall, only if qualified, written net after travel replaces fees and transport fits.
Keep **supervised pupils** until a suitable written offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a realistic fee loss.
S1.quote: I would not pretend I can teach a new system in a weekend.
fieldNote: Her **association request** protects real paid preparation and class hours.
She sets **strict tool conditions** for privacy and checking but does not commit to learning AI this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre that AGI by 2028 may make practice beats for pennies. I would ask whether the human assistant and the Friday class are still paid, in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the recording fees to end in 2028 and worry that the centre will cut assistant hours too. Robots that can handle instruments come around 2031, three years later, but I could lose most of my small wage before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would count the practice-track invoices and ask for a signed Friday schedule. In the first year after 2028, if paid class hours also fall, I would apply for a posted library music-room aide job only if my secondary education qualifies, its written net pay after travel covers lost class fees and the hours fit our shared transport; I would keep the current centre work until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the likely recording loss; I would be alarmed if class fees also shrank. I have lain awake asking how we would cover rent without even one month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a course before applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would study only if the posted aide job requires it and training is funded or paid time is offered. Our last weeks of savings cannot pay tuition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you rely on retirement soon?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot assume a pension amount I have not checked. I would ask for a written benefits statement while keeping paid work.

say: I would warn the centre that **practice beats** may become very cheap by 2028.
I would ask for **written Friday pay** for the human assistant and class.
think: **Recording fees** likely end in 2028 before 2031 robots.
Lost **assistant hours** could remove most of my wage.
do: Count **practice invoices** and request a signed Friday schedule now.
Apply for **posted aide work** after 2028 class cuts if qualified; written net after travel covers losses, transport fits.
Keep **paid centre work** until written offer; request written benefits statement; study only for posted requirements with funded tuition or paid time.
feel: I feel **anxious** about likely recording losses; additional class or live-call cuts would alarm me.
S2.quote: Our last weeks of savings cannot pay tuition.
fieldNote: She faces **2028 recording loss** before hands-on robots around 2031.
The **library move** needs actual class cuts, a qualified posted job, written net replacement, transport and signed offer.

steps.text: Count paid practice-track invoices and request signed Friday schedule now
Apply for qualified posted aide after cuts; written net after travel covers class loss, transport fits
Keep paid centre work until written offer; request written benefits statement without assuming pension
Take required aide course only for posted job with funded tuition or paid study time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell parents that five years until AGI by 2031 gives us time to see if a small paid hand-drum group will work. I would not ask a senior tutor to supervise for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Practice recordings may go by 2031, and drumming robots may appear around 2034. I could earn a group fee, but only if families pay before we book the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would ask the centre to let me help run a six-week beginner group only if the senior tutor agrees to supervise, the room hire terms are confirmed in writing and eight families prepay enough for room hire, inspected loan drums, the tutor’s paid time and my teaching and preparation. In the first year after 2031 I would repeat only if those eight fees still cover both wages including my preparation, a safe room and safe drums; otherwise I would keep the current pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious until both teachers are paid. With our small reserve, I will not fund a class by skipping groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who makes sure the drums are safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre technician must inspect rims and stands before children touch them. If a drum fails, the child brings a safe one or we find a safe replacement booking that preserves eight paid places; otherwise we defer the group and refund all deposits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four families pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees do not pay the tutor, room and my preparation. I would refund them and keep the regular paid sessions.

I would refuse to ask the **senior tutor** to supervise for free.
think: Eight **prepaid places** could replace some recording fees after the room and both teachers are paid.
do: Start the **beginner group** with written room terms, tutor supervision and eight prepayments covering inspected drums, room, both wages and preparation.
Repeat **after 2031** only while eight fees cover those costs; replace unsafe places safely or defer/refund everyone.
Keep **current paid pupils** and refund four deposits if too few families pay.
feel: I feel **anxious** because thin savings cannot fund a class.
S3.quote: I will not fund a class by skipping groceries.
fieldNote: The **group gate** includes senior-tutor supervision, eight prepayments, room, inspected drums and both adults’ time.
An **unsafe drum** requires a safe replacement preserving eight paid places or deferral and full refunds.

steps.text: Start supervised group: written room, eight prepayments cover inspected drums, room, both wages/preparation
Repeat after 2031 on same floor; replace unsafe places safely or defer/refund all

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the centre committee that a decade until AGI by 2036 is time to write down wages and training, not just promise volunteers a future. I will be 68 then, and I still need a pay plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Recording work may end by 2036 and robots could handle drums around 2039. Our thin savings and a small junior wage make the next year harder than the ten-year headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this term I would ask for a written two-year paid assistant agreement and save five percent of each extra paid weekend lesson after rent, food and transport, aiming for two months. In the first year after 2036, if music fees fall, I would keep paid classes and apply for a posted centre music aide role only if my secondary schooling qualifies, written net pay after travel covers lost recording and class fees and the hours fit shared transport; I would leave only after a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would remain anxious because a contract can end long before 2036. Having ten years does not turn an empty savings account into a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra weekend lessons come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save nothing new that week. I would not label grocery money as spare income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you checked retirement income?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I would ask for a written estimate, but I would not stop paid work on the strength of a guess.

say: I would ask the committee to write down **wages and training** during the decade.
I would say I still need a **pay plan** at 68 in 2036.
think: **Recording fees** may end by 2036 before 2039 drum robots.
Our **thin reserve** makes current income the urgent issue.
do: Request a **written two-year paid agreement** and pension estimate this term.
Save five percent of **extra paid lessons** after rent, food and transport toward two months.
Apply for **posted aide** after 2036 music losses if qualified; written net after travel covers losses, transport fits; stay until signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about current wages despite the longer runway.
S4.quote: Having ten years does not turn an empty savings account into a pension.
fieldNote: Her **two-month goal** uses only extra paid lessons after essentials.
The **later aide move** requires a qualified posted job, written net replacement, transport and signed offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because practice-track fees and assistant hours could go before I find another job. Signed paid Fridays, a real aide opening with fair net pay and transport that works would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether anyone is paid to watch the youngest drummer. A class needs an adult who is there on purpose, not by accident.

headlineQuote: A class needs an adult who is there on purpose, not by accident.
portrait: At **58**, Sara is a junior hand drummer who came from laundry work and finished secondary school.
Her **lower pay**, under-one-month reserve and few local posts make lost class hours frightening; she seeks a written pension estimate.
She has **never used AI** and does not commit to a tool trial without paid instruction, privacy and senior-tutor checks.
A **paid beginner group** needs supervision, eight prepayments, a room, safe drums and pay for both adults.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase practice-track fees and assistant hours before another paid job opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed paid Fridays**, a qualified posted aide job with sufficient net pay and workable transport would help Sara.
